Atypical prosody is a recognized clinical feature of autism and has been widely investigated as a potential marker for automated screening. However, findings have been difficult to replicate across languages and tasks, raising questions about whether there is a generalizable “autistic voice.” We asked whether acoustic differences vary with children’s development and individual skills, rather than reflecting diagnosis alone. Speakers in many languages show a processing bias for consonants in word learning and recognition (C-bias). Infants learning such languages initially display an opposite bias for vowels (V-bias), switching to the C-bias through experience with native phono-lexical properties. In French-learning infants, this switch happens between 6 and 8 months. Here we asked whether early phonetic production is linked to this developmental pattern. Thirty-one French-learning 7-month-olds completed a wordform segmentation task testing consonant-vowel perceptual biases, daylong recordings (LENA system), and parental questionnaires. item.title: Updated: Dependency or Phrase Structure Grammars
item.dc:creator: Müller, Stefan
item.description:
Müller, Stefan · LingBuzz

It is often claimed that Dependency Grammar (DG) is simpler than phrase structure grammars. Gibson (2026a) even made this claim quite explicitly in the title of his paper "Dependency syntax as the simplest theory of grammar". This answer to Gibson's paper shows that DGs appear simpler since many aspects of a formal theory are simply not provided. Many DGs come without a rule component. I discuss the rules the Gibson provides in a syntax textbook and show that they are formally not sound and that they mimic phrase structure-based systems in their intention. Treating semantics requires more structure either in terms of nodes or in terms of additional features. Any apparent advantage of DGs is …

Bilingualism is a multidimensional, dynamic construct that is challenging to measure. Common bilingualism questionnaires differ in the items they contain, complicating comparisons across studies. Prior work has shown limited content overlap between questionnaire items, but the extent of conceptual, or latent overlap between questionnaires remains unclear. We assessed conceptual overlap among seven bilingualism questionnaires by analyzing participant responses rather than questionnaire content. We administered all seven questionnaires to French-English and English-French sequential bilingual undergraduates. item.description:
David M. Amodio; Tessa Elizabeth Sadie Charlesworth; William J. Brady · PsyArXiv

Algorithmic bias—the systematic discrimination of disadvantaged social groups by AI systems—is widely documented, yet its psychological foundations remain poorly understood. We argue that algorithmic bias originates primarily from human prejudice and social cognition, which shape AI training data and use of AI systems. We introduce the psychology-centered Human–AI Loop model that explains how biases can enter an AI system during its creation and consumption, specifying the psychological mechanisms operating at each entry point. These mechanisms and their interactions create feedback loops through which AI systems amplify, perpetuate, and obscure existing prejudices and social inequalities. …

item.title: Updated: The limited utility of metaphors in ecology and evolutionary biology
item.dc:creator: Ernesto Gianoli
Aaron M. Ellison
item.description:
Ernesto Gianoli; Aaron M. Ellison · SocArXiv

Metaphors are deeply embedded in ecology and evolutionary biology. They help scientists communicate unfamiliar ideas, generate hypotheses, and organize complex phenomena into intuitive conceptual frameworks. Consequently, metaphors have often been portrayed as indispensable tools for scientific progress. Here, we argue that this view is only partly correct. Although metaphors can stimulate discovery during the early stages of research, their continued use as research areas mature can become counterproductive. Through examples drawn from ecology, evolutionary biology, philosophy of science, and the history of biology, we show how metaphors simplify complex phenomena, encourage reification, …

The wrap-up effect, i.e., the inflation of reading times on sentence- or clause-final words relative to preceding words, is a robust finding in reading research, typically interpreted to reflect integrative processing of meaning. However, recent cross-linguistic evidence has cast doubt on its generalizability across languages, raising questions about the mechanisms that underlie it. Here, we test an information-theoretic account of the wrap-up effect, according to which the effect reflects readers’ adaptive behavior to where semantic information resides in their written language. Why did closely related North Germanic varieties undergo different trajectories during the medieval long back vowel shift (Stora Vokaldansen)? While Swedish and much of Norwegian underwent successive raising of /ɑː/, /oː/, and /uː/, Danish underwent only the initial rounding of /ɑː/ to /ɔː/. Einar Haugen (1970) concluded that this divergence admitted no structural explanation and had to be extra-linguistic. Using the Pressure-Resistance-Actuation (PRA) framework, this squib argues that early, pervasive unstressed vowel reduction in Danish concentrated contrastive information within the stressed syllable, increasing systemic resistance to further vowel reorganisation. It has long been known that there is much dialectal variation among tense forms in English irregular verbs, particularly among the simple past and past participle forms. Such variation has often been analysed as analogical levelling, whereby the past participle usually levels towards the simple past forms (e.g., I spoke/have spoke). This paper argues that, for North East English, explanations based on levelling do not capture the complexity of the non-standard paradigms, some of which have not levelled at all but have, using the terminology of Lass, ‘crossed over’ (e.g., I sung/have sang). item.dc:creator: Radim Lacina
Utku Turk
item.description:
Radim Lacina; Utku Turk · PsyArXiv + LingBuzz

This is a review of Dan Parker's book 'Linguistic illusions: A case study on agreement attraction' published by Cambridge University Press in 2025. The book gives a comprehensive summary of both the basics of a myriad of illusory phenomena and of agreement attraction in detail. It is a valuable resource for students and researchers alike, especially thanks to the accessible explanations of the leading issues and theories in the field. We critically discuss the book's reported ACT-R modelling, original experiments and its limited engagement with the cross-linguistic study of attraction.

In this study, we examine two Mandarin fricative contrasts that are variably merged in Quanzhou Southern Min–Mandarin bilingual speech. The Mandarin /f/∼/x/ contrast contains a sound /f/ that is absent from Southern Min but that can be assimilated to /hw/, making it distinct from /x/. Bilingual vocabulary size is often compared with monolingual scores, especially when bilingual normative data are not available, but there is no agreement on how to measure it. Bilingual scores commonly rely on a single language score, on the total amount of words known across languages (total vocabulary) or on the sum of concepts known in either language (conceptual vocabulary). item.title: Can Chimpanzees Imagine a Blue Banana?
item.dc:creator: Andrey Vyshedskiy
item.description:
Andrey Vyshedskiy · PsyArXiv

Can a chimpanzee that has learned words for colors and objects find a blue pencil among pencils, straws, and Lego pieces in red, green, and blue? This seemingly simple task requires more than recognizing individual words: it requires integrating the meaning of a color adjective with that of a noun to identify an object possessing both properties. Children typically master this ability by 2.3 years. By age 3, they can integrate two modifiers, such as size and color, to follow instructions like “Find a large green straw.” These achievements mark important milestones in the development of language comprehension, allowing children to combine multiple words into a unified mental representation …

Gender and number features are frequently co-expressed within a single exponent, and when realised separately, gender morphology tends to surface closer to the stem. This paper audits the evidence for lexical contact between Ishakkoy (Atakapa), a language isolate of the Gulf Coast, and Louisiana French Creole, Louisiana's French-lexified Creole. Ishakkoy has no known relatives, so no word the two languages share can have come down from a common ancestor.
